titulo.texto: Model of the Circular Platform of Cuicuilco

frase_gancho.texto: A circular city that the volcano buried under lava.

puente_narrativo.texto: With the people of Cuicuilco on the march north, move on to the Teotihuacán Hall: there rose the great city that, according to many, welcomed those refugees.

guion_corto.texto: This scale model shows the Great Circular Platform of Cuicuilco, the main building of the first great city of the Central Highlands. Its circular form, with stairways and ramps that climbed through stepped tiers to a temple at the top, measured more than a hundred meters in diameter and rose to the height of a building of about seven stories. Cuicuilco came to have more than twenty thousand inhabitants, canals to irrigate the fields, and highly elaborate ceremonies. Until the Xitle volcano erupted, in the early centuries of our era, and covered the city with a layer of lava several meters thick. Today that black rock is called the Pedregal de San Ángel, and the pyramid can be visited.

guion_largo.texto:
Look at the model slowly and try to imagine the city it represents. There are no corners. The main monument of Cuicuilco, between the year six hundred before Christ and the early centuries of our era, was a circular platform of several tiers that grew smaller as they rose, like a gigantic wedding cake. People climbed by broad ramps and stairways, and at the top stood a temple made of perishable materials, with altars where offerings were made. For specialists, the round shape is no accident: it symbolizes the horizon, the sun, and the sacred mountain from which water springs.

Cuicuilco was an extraordinary city for its time. Its inhabitants numbered more than twenty thousand, they had canals to carry water from the springs to the fields, and a monumental ceremonial center. For several centuries it was the most important place in the Valley of Mexico, a serious rival to the city that would later surpass it, Teotihuacán.

Then came the event that changed everything. To the south of the city rises the Xitle volcano, and in the early centuries of our era it erupted. The lava flowed down the slope and covered fields, houses, and temples under a layer of rock that, in some places, reaches several meters in thickness and that altogether covers about eighty square kilometers. Cuicuilco was buried. We do not know how many people died, but we do know that the survivors had to leave.

Here there is a much-repeated hypothesis: that many of those refugees went north, toward Teotihuacán, and that their arrival helped that city grow into a metropolis. Archaeologists still debate how much the volcano mattered and how much other factors did, but the story is so powerful that it is worth telling: one city falls and another lifts its head.

And the pyramid of Cuicuilco was discovered by chance and thanks to a great idea. In the 1920s, the American archaeologist Byron Cummings dug beneath the lava and, with pickaxes and even explosives, opened a crack in the rock. Beneath it appeared this circular structure, which had remained hidden for almost two thousand years. Since then, other archaeologists have studied and restored it.

The model serves precisely for that: to let us see what the lava and time no longer allow us to see. At the top, it is thought that worship was offered to the Old God of Fire, the clay elder you have just seen, and to the god of rain. Fire and water, on top of an artificial mountain, at the foot of a real volcano.

One last practical recommendation. The pyramid of Cuicuilco is not just a model: you can visit it, in the south of Mexico City, on Insurgentes Avenue, and walk around it with the black of the Pedregal on either side. And if you notice, as you finish this hall, the museum takes you exactly along that path: from Cuicuilco, which falls, to Teotihuacán, which rises.

texto: Count the stepped tiers of the model and look for the ramps that climb to the top
Notice the circular shape, with no corners
Imagine the lava from Xitle covering everything up to the edge of the pyramid

texto.pregunta: Myth: The pyramid of Cuicuilco was built by the Mexica and was made for sacrifices.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is much older than the Mexica; it is the great monument of a Preclassic city more than two thousand years old, which was buried by the lava of the Xitle volcano.
